title: Quality Indicators & Continuous Improvement
shortDescription: The PDCA cycle and the vocabulary of ongoing improvement — indicator, target, benchmark, trend — applied to a lab example and a hospital example.
genZNote: Plan, Do, Check, Act. Four words, and basically the whole philosophy of this subject.

sections.heading: The Vocabulary of Improvement
bullets: Quality indicator — a measurable element used to track quality over time.
Target — the specific value an organisation aims to reach for an indicator.
Benchmark — a reference point, often an external best-practice value, used for comparison.
Trend — the direction an indicator is moving over multiple time periods, not just one snapshot.
Monitoring — the ongoing act of tracking an indicator.
Variance — the gap between actual performance and the target or expected value.
Corrective action — fixing an identified problem after it occurs.
Preventive/risk-based action — acting on a potential problem BEFORE it occurs, based on identified risk.

sections.heading: The PDCA Cycle
sections.body: Plan-Do-Check-Act is the underlying improvement logic running through nearly every process in this subject — NABL's accreditation cycle, NABH's incident-to-improvement workflow, and hospital quality management from Chapter 11 are all specific applications of this same generic pattern.

steps.name: Plan
steps.explanation: Identify a problem or improvement opportunity, and plan a specific change to address it.
steps.purpose: Nothing gets fixed by accident — the change has to be deliberately designed.

steps.name: Do
steps.explanation: Implement the planned change, ideally on a small/controlled scale first.
steps.purpose: Tests the change before committing to it fully.

steps.name: Check
steps.explanation: Measure whether the change actually produced the intended result.
steps.purpose: Separates 'we made a change' from 'the change worked'.

steps.name: Act
steps.explanation: If it worked, standardise and scale it. If not, adjust the plan and cycle again.
steps.purpose: Turns a successful trial into the new normal — or sends you back to Plan with better information.

sections.heading: Two Worked Examples
sections.body:
Laboratory example: a lab notices its turnaround time for a critical test is trending upward (variance from target). It PLANS a workflow change, DOES it on the night shift first, CHECKS whether turnaround time actually improved, and ACTS by rolling it out to all shifts once confirmed.

Hospital example: a hospital's surgical site infection rate benchmark is being missed. It PLANS a revised pre-operative antiseptic protocol, DOES a pilot on one surgical ward, CHECKS the infection rate on that ward over the following weeks, and ACTS by extending the protocol hospital-wide once the data confirms improvement.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Continuous improvement in laboratories and hospitals runs on the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle, applied to measurable quality indicators tracked against targets, benchmarks, and trends over time.
keyFacts: PDCA = Plan, Do, Check, Act — a repeating cycle, not a one-time sequence.
A benchmark is typically an external reference point; a target is the organisation's own internal goal.
Trend requires multiple data points over time — a single measurement can't show a trend.
Corrective action responds to a problem that already occurred; preventive/risk-based action addresses a risk before it does.
commonConfusion: Corrective action and preventive/risk-based action are often blurred together — corrective action responds to something that has already happened; preventive action addresses a risk before it materialises.

highYieldFacts: PDCA is a CYCLE — 'Act' typically feeds back into a new 'Plan', not a stopping point.
A target is internally set; a benchmark is typically an external comparison point.
commonTraps: Treating PDCA as a one-time linear project rather than a repeating cycle.
Confusing corrective action (after the fact) with preventive/risk-based action (before the fact).
mustRemember: Plan → Do → Check → Act → back to Plan.

confusedTerms.distinction: Corrective action addresses a problem that has already occurred, to stop it recurring. Preventive/risk-based action addresses an identified risk before any problem has occurred.

possibleQuestions: Apply the PDCA cycle to a quality problem in either a laboratory or a hospital setting, with a concrete example at each stage.

pathways.title: The PDCA Cycle
steps: Plan — identify the problem, design a specific change
Do — implement the change, ideally on a small scale first
Check — measure whether it actually worked
Act — standardise if successful, or adjust and cycle again

questions.prompt: In the PDCA cycle, what comes immediately after 'Do'?
questions.explanation: The cycle runs Plan → Do → Check → Act.

questions.prompt: A hospital sees its surgical infection rate rising and revises its pre-op protocol as a pilot on one ward before rolling it out further. This pilot stage corresponds to which PDCA phase?
questions.explanation: Piloting the implemented change on a controlled scale is the 'Do' phase.
